summary: Defines QPACK, a compression format for efficiently representing HTTP header and trailer fields in HTTP/3. It is a variation of HPACK and aims to reduce head-of-line blocking. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Repeated words in messages get replaced by short codes, and the system does not make everyone wait when one piece is late.

questions: how does qpack avoid head of line blocking
what are qpack encoder and decoder streams
subtitle: How HTTP/3 shrinks repeated header fields without making every request wait on a lost packet.

tldr.problem: HTTP/2 compresses header and trailer fields with HPACK, which assumes one totally ordered sequence of frames. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, where streams can arrive out of order, so HPACK would cause head-of-line blocking.
tldr.mechanism: QPACK keeps HPACK's static and dynamic tables but sends table updates on separate one-way encoder and decoder streams. Each encoded field section states which table state it needs, so the decoder knows whether it can decode it now or must wait.
tldr.outcome: QPACK lets implementations trade compression ratio against blocking risk. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 9204 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2022, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines QPACK for HTTP/3.

sections.title: Why HTTP/3 Needs a New Compressor
sections.content:
HTTP/2 compresses header and trailer sections with HPACK (RFC 7541). HPACK has built-in assumptions of a total ordering across frames on all streams. HTTP/3 runs on QUIC, which does not guarantee order between data on different streams, so using HPACK there would induce head-of-line blocking for field sections.

QPACK reuses the core concepts of HPACK but is redesigned to stay correct when data arrives out of order. The stated design goals are to closely approach the compression ratio of HPACK with substantially less head-of-line blocking under the same loss conditions. The RFC notes that QPACK is a name, not an abbreviation.

The RFC uses the word fields for what people colloquially call headers. A field section is the ordered collection of field lines (name-value pairs) belonging to one HTTP message, and both header and trailer sections count.
sections.plainLanguage: The old shortcut system only worked if every note arrived in order. The internet for HTTP/3 can deliver notes out of order, so QPACK is a shortcut system that still works when notes show up late.

sections.title: Encoder, Decoder and Two Streams
sections.content:
An encoder turns each header or trailer section into a series of representations, either an indexed one (a reference to a table entry) or a literal one. It MUST emit them in the order the field lines appear in the input, and the decoder MUST emit them in the same order. QPACK puts the burden of optional state tracking on the encoder, which keeps decoders relatively simple.

Unlike HPACK, table changes do not travel inside the encoded field sections. QPACK defines two unidirectional stream types instead:

  • The encoder stream (type 0x02) carries encoder instructions from encoder to decoder.
  • The decoder stream (type 0x03) carries decoder instructions from decoder to encoder.

Each HTTP/3 endpoint contains both an encoder and a decoder and MUST initiate at most one stream of each type. A second instance is a connection error of type H3_STREAM_CREATION_ERROR, and closing either stream is a connection error of type H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM. An endpoint MAY skip creating a stream it will not use, for example when the dynamic table maximum is zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing new nicknames in the middle of each message, the two sides use two private walkie-talkies. One is for announcing new nicknames, the other for saying which ones have been heard.

sections.title: The Static and Dynamic Tables
sections.content:
QPACK has two tables that are addressed separately. The static table is a predefined list of common field lines (some with an empty value) with fixed indices; QPACK indexes it from 0, whereas HPACK indexes its static table from 1. The dynamic table is a first-in, first-out list that starts empty and is built up during the connection by the encoder.

The size of a dynamic table entry is the length of its name in bytes plus the length of its value in bytes plus 32 additional bytes, measured without Huffman encoding. The encoder sets the table capacity, which starts at zero, using a Set Dynamic Table Capacity instruction. The decoder bounds the capacity the encoder may choose with SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY. New entries push out old ones from the end of the table, but an entry can only be evicted when it is evictable, meaning its insertion has been acknowledged and no unacknowledged field section still references it.

Three kinds of index are used:

  • Absolute index: fixed for the life of the entry, starting at 0 for the first entry inserted.
  • Relative index: counts back from the newest entry on the encoder stream, or from the field section's Base in a field line representation.
  • Post-Base index: counts forward from the Base, so an encoder can reference entries it inserted while encoding the same field section in a single pass.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a printed list of common phrases that never changes, and a notebook that grows as you talk. Each notebook line gets a permanent number so both sides always point at the same line.

sections.title: Blocked Streams and Staying in Sync
sections.content:
Because QUIC does not order data across streams, a decoder may receive a field section that refers to a table entry it has not yet seen. Each encoded field section therefore carries a Required Insert Count: one more than the largest absolute index it references, or zero if it uses no dynamic entries. If that is greater than the decoder's own Insert Count (the total number of entries inserted so far), the stream is blocked until the missing entries arrive.

The decoder limits blocking with SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS, and the encoder MUST NOT risk more blocked streams than that. An encoder can avoid all risk by referencing only acknowledged entries, at the cost of sending more literals, which makes field sections bigger. That is the trade-off QPACK leaves to implementations.

The decoder reports progress on the decoder stream. A Section Acknowledgment says a field section has been fully decoded, a Stream Cancellation says a stream was reset or abandoned, and an Insert Count Increment says how many more table insertions have been processed. The encoder tracks the Known Received Count, the total number of insertions and duplications the decoder has acknowledged, to know which entries are safe to reference without blocking.

To avoid references that would pin old entries and stop new insertions, the encoder can emit a Duplicate instruction and reference the copy. The RFC also warns that an encoder SHOULD NOT write an instruction unless enough flow-control credit is available for all of it, to avoid deadlocks.
sections.plainLanguage: If a note says use nickname number 9 but you have not heard nickname 9 yet, you set the note aside and wait. The listener also sends back little thank-you messages so the speaker knows which nicknames are safe to use.

sections.title: Instructions and Field Line Representations
sections.content:
Everything on the wire is built from HPACK's prefixed integers and string literals (with optional Huffman coding), reused unmodified, except that a string literal may now start mid-byte with a prefix between 2 and 8 bits. Implementations MUST be able to decode integers up to and including 62 bits long.

Encoder instructions change the dynamic table: Set Dynamic Table Capacity (pattern 001), Insert with Name Reference (1), Insert with Literal Name (01) and Duplicate (000). Decoder instructions report state: Section Acknowledgment (1), Stream Cancellation (01) and Insert Count Increment (00).

Each encoded field section starts with a prefix of two integers: the Required Insert Count (transformed modulo twice the maximum number of entries, so the prefix stays short on long connections) and a sign bit plus Delta Base that together give the Base. As the RFC's example, with a Required Insert Count of 9, a Sign bit of 1 and a Delta Base of 2, the Base is 6.

After the prefix come the field line representations: Indexed Field Line, Indexed Field Line with Post-Base Index, Literal Field Line with Name Reference, Literal Field Line with Post-Base Name Reference, and Literal Field Line with Literal Name. Representations only read table state; they never modify it.
sections.plainLanguage: Every little message starts with a few secret bits that say what kind of message it is, like the first letter on a coded note. Reading those bits tells you whether to add a nickname, thank the speaker, or look one up.

sections.title: Settings and Error Codes
sections.content:
QPACK adds two settings to the HTTP/3 SETTINGS frame, both defaulting to zero:

  • SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY (0x01), the equivalent of HTTP/2's SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE.
  • SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS (0x07), the most streams that may be blocked.

Because both default to zero, the dynamic table is unused until the peer's SETTINGS frame says otherwise. When the maximum capacity is zero, the encoder MUST NOT insert entries or send encoder instructions. The RFC also describes special handling when a client uses 0-RTT data and remembers the server's earlier setting value.

Three error codes cover QPACK failures: QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED (0x0200), QPACK_ENCODER_STREAM_ERROR (0x0201) and QPACK_DECODER_STREAM_ERROR (0x0202). Invalid references, such as to an evicted entry or a bad static index, are connection errors.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides start with the notebook switched off. Each side has to say how big a notebook it can handle and how many messages it can keep on hold before the shortcuts are used.

sections.title: Compression Side Channels and Memory Limits
sections.content:
The main concern is that compression can leak secrets. An attacker who can choose fields to be encoded and observe the encoded length can confirm guesses about the dynamic table, because a correct guess compresses to something shorter. TLS and QUIC protect content but only limit protection of its length. The RFC cites attacks such as CRIME as proof of this capability.

QPACK mitigates but does not completely prevent such attacks, because a guess must match an entire field line rather than a character at a time. Low-entropy values remain vulnerable, and the danger appears whenever mutually distrustful entities share one HTTP/3 connection, for example behind an intermediary or among web origins in a browser.

Two tools help. Implementations can segregate access to the dynamic table by the entity building the message. And the never-indexed literal, signalled by the N bit, tells intermediaries not to index a value: an intermediary MUST NOT re-encode such a value in a way that would index it. Encoders might choose this for fields like Cookie or Authorization.

For memory, the table capacity and blocked-stream settings bound what an encoder can make a decoder hold. Implementations also need limits for large integers and long string literals.
sections.plainLanguage: If a spy can watch how short your coded message gets, they can guess the secret word by trying words until the message shrinks. So very private words are written out in full and never turned into nicknames.

items.label: Set Dynamic Table Capacity
items.desc: Changes the table capacity; not acknowledged.

items.label: Insert with Name Reference
items.desc: Adds an entry whose name comes from the static or dynamic table.

items.label: Insert with Literal Name
items.desc: Adds an entry with both name and value as string literals.

items.label: Duplicate
items.desc: Reinserts an existing entry without resending name or value.

items.desc: A field section with dynamic references has been processed.

items.label: Stream Cancellation
items.desc: A stream was reset or reading was abandoned.

items.label: Insert Count Increment
items.desc: Raises the Known Received Count by the Increment value.
